absent: Layouts and semantics of task, completion, mutex, pipe, watch, queue, list, notification, credential and signal structures beyond field uses shown.
Thread creation, scheduling, sleep and wakeup, signal delivery, and exit behavior beyond the call sites shown.
Expansion and wire format of crash metadata recording macros and note publication and log-buffer setup.
Numeric values and limits for crash buffer sizes, hardware-error table size, page orders, section and zone constants, and watch type counts.
Security policy for notification posting and credential and resource-limit enforcement details.
Pipe ring, buffer accounting, resize, poll, async notification, and file-descriptor handling internals.
Architecture-specific crash hook implementations and safe-copy usage.

findings.text: Vhost worker lifecycle exposes creation with work and kill callbacks plus owner data and name, separate start to make the thread runnable, explicit wake, and orderly stop that frees the descriptor after thread exit.

Vhost worker descriptor groups two owner callbacks and opaque owner data with an exit completion, a flag word for stop and killed conditions, a thread reference, and a mutex that arbitrates termination.

Worker thread alternates between fatal-signal handling, stop recognition, delegated work, and interruptible sleep. Termination distinguishes orderly stop from externally killed, invoking the kill callback only when stop was not already requested, then signals exit and terminates.
A dedicated exit mutex serializes the stop path against the signal-driven kill path so only one termination outcome wins and the kill handler cannot run after orderly stop began.

Creation requests a thread sharing filesystem, address space, threads and signal handling in untraced user-worker mode without files, initializes completion and mutex before thread creation, and on allocation or thread-creation failure releases what was allocated and reports an error pointer.

Crash metadata initialization runs once at boot, reserves zeroed areas for human-readable metadata and for the note, records operating system release, page size, selected symbols, structure sizes and field offsets, memory-model parameters and page-type tags, invokes an architecture hook, then publishes the note.
Crash metadata state comprises a data buffer pointer with size, a note pointer, a private safe copy pointer, and a hardware-error table whose entries each pair a counter with a timestamp.
Hardware-error logging silently ignores a source outside the valid table range; otherwise it increments that source counter and records current real time.
Architecture-specific crash metadata hook defaults to a weak empty operation that implementations elsewhere may override.
Watch queue note storage unit is 128 bytes.
Number of watch notes fitting in one page equals page size divided by note size.
Queue access uses a bottom-half protected spinlock; acquisition succeeds only while the queue remains attached to a pipe, otherwise it releases and reports failure, with a paired unlock.
Watch pipe buffers use custom release handling that returns the backing note slot to the free set, forbid stealing, and share generic acquisition behavior.

Notification posting either publishes one entry into a free preallocated slot and wakes readers and asynchronous waiters, or when the pipe is full or no slot is free marks loss on the newest entry without adding data.
Filtering requires the notification type to be enabled and at least one per-type rule whose subtype bit is set and whose masked info value matches; when any filter exists the default is rejection.

Broadcast walks subscribed watches under read-side protection, selects matching identifiers, personalizes identifier bits per watcher, applies per-queue filter and security policy, and posts to each still-attached queue.

Queue sizing is one-time only, bounds the requested note count, checks pipe buffer accounting and privilege limits, grows the note count to whole pages, resizes the ring, then allocates backing pages and an initially full free bitmap.

Queue filter installation copies a user descriptor, validates count and reserved fields and masked info constraints, ignores unknown types, builds a compact kernel filter, and swaps it under pipe lock with deferred reclamation of the old filter; a null descriptor clears filtering.

Watch list mutation nests list lock inside queue lock on the add path, while removal and teardown drop the queue lock before acquiring list locks and detach the pipe first, avoiding deadlock between posters and removers and preventing new posts during teardown.

Watch and queue objects use reference counts with read-copy-update delayed destruction; final release frees backing pages, bitmap, filter and descriptor for queues, and releases queue reference, credential, per-user watch count and memory for watches.

Watch management initializes queue linkage, enforces at most one binding per queue and identifier with per-user file-count limit, supports targeted or full removal with a removal notification and optional release callback, resolves queues from file descriptors, creates queues on pipes, and detaches all watches on teardown.
Publishing treats a missing free-slot bit at commit time as a fatal inconsistency, and broadcasting drops zero-length notifications with a warning.

Callers observe distinct failures for missing queue, already sized queue, out-of-range sizes, permission and memory exhaustion, bad user memory and bad filter parameters, duplicate watch binding, watch-count overflow, missing removal target, worker allocation failure, and crash-buffer allocation failure.
Page mapcount tag values encode slab, buddy, huge-page, offline and unaccepted page-type tags in a high-order byte for crash analysis.
